title: CPP Disability Benefits
subtitle: Build a work-capacity record that connects the medical and employment evidence

blocks.text: A medical chart can explain a condition beautifully and still forget to mention why Tuesday’s four-hour shift became impossible.

The Canada Pension Plan disability benefit is a taxable monthly payment for people over 18 and under 65 who paid into CPP and whose disability is both severe and prolonged under CPP law. Severe means you regularly cannot do any job that pays a real living, not only your old job. Prolonged means long-term with no end date, or likely to result in death.

In 2026, work that pays a real living means earning $20,971.45 a year or more before tax. Earnings are one piece of proof. Service Canada looks at the whole picture of what you can do, how often and what work you have tried.

items.title: “Being unable to return to my old occupation automatically meets the CPP disability test.”
items.text: The test asks whether you can regularly do any job that pays a real living, based on all the evidence. CPP does not stop its job search at the old staff directory.

blocks.text: Knowing the two gates CPP disability checks keeps a strong medical file from failing on a missing link.
blocks.detail: Your health, your daily limits and your work history all have to tell one connected story.
blocks.extra: Section 02 separates the medical gate from the contribution gate.

sections.title: The Medical Test and Your CPP Payments Are Separate Gates

blocks.text: The first gate is about your health and work: your condition must regularly stop you from doing any job that pays a real living, and it must be long-term with no end date, or likely to result in death. Your age, schooling, language, work history, treatment, limits and attempts to work can all help explain what you can do.

The second gate is your CPP payments. You usually need to have paid into CPP in four of the six years before you became disabled, or for at least 25 years, including three of the last six. Rules for late applicants may help if your payment record stopped counting before you applied.
Check your CPP Statement of Contributions early. Medical proof cannot replace missing CPP payments, and a strong payment record cannot replace the severe-and-prolonged test.
If you paid into the Quebec Pension Plan, you may need to apply through QPP disability. Living in Quebec now does not by itself show which plan your payments went to.

items.title: “A DTC approval automatically means CPP disability approval.”
items.text: The two programs use different legal tests. The DTC looks at limits on daily tasks for a tax credit. CPP disability looks at whether you can regularly work at a job that pays a real living, plus your CPP payments.

sections.title: Connect Your Condition, Your Limits and Your Work

items.title: MEDICAL EVIDENCE
items.text: Diagnosis, history, test results where they matter, treatment, how you responded, outlook and how long it is expected to last.

items.title: DAILY LIMITS
items.text: What you can do reliably, for how long and how often, including rest time, supervision, changes at work or help from others.

items.title: WORK EVIDENCE
items.text: What your job asked of you, missed days, cut hours, changed duties, failed returns, changes at work and why you stopped.

items.title: OTHER WORK YOU COULD DO
items.text: Your schooling, language and skills, and whether you could do other paying work regularly, not just once on a good day.

blocks.text: Send your part of the application right away. Do not wait for the medical report. Service Canada needs both parts before it decides, but the date it gets your application can affect how far back payments go.

If you are approved, payment usually starts four months after the date your disability is found severe and prolonged. Back pay can cover up to 11 months before the date Service Canada received your application.

items.title: “More pages of medical records always make a stronger application.”
items.text: Clear, consistent proof beats volume. A 300-page chart that never explains what you can do at work may be a heavy mystery novel.

blocks.text: CPP disability needs enough CPP payments plus proof that your condition regularly stops you from any job that pays a real living, for a long time.

sections.title: Samira and the File With No Bridge

paragraphs: Samira Haddad runs a warehouse shift in Edmonton. A long-term nerve condition has made the job harder every month. Her goal is to apply for CPP disability before her savings run out in the fall.

Her first draft names her diagnosis and attaches every specialist report. It says almost nothing about her actual work. It skips the missed shifts, the pace she could no longer keep safely and the two days she needed to recover after a short trial return.
A co-worker who was turned down warns her. “They said my file proved I was sick. It didn’t prove I couldn’t work.”

Samira has a choice. She could send the thick folder now and hope the reports speak for themselves. Or she could spend a week writing down how her condition hits her work, day by day. She decides to do both: she sends her part of the application that day, so the date counts, and she starts the work record that night.

She lists her hours, absences, the changes her boss made and every return that failed. Her doctor adds treatment, outlook and her limits. Samira also checks her CPP record and finds enough years of payments.

The twist comes at her doctor’s office. The doctor points out that her limits would rule out desk work too, because she cannot sit or focus for long stretches. Samira had never thought to say that. It goes in the file.
Service Canada makes the decision. But her file now shows how the condition affects reliable work, instead of asking a diagnosis to carry the entire file.

blocks.text: A failed return to work can matter when you write down the duties, hours, changes, symptoms, recovery time and why it ended. It is not automatic proof either way.
Samira sent her application right away and then built the work record that connected her reports to her job.
blocks.detail: The same three-part file can show Service Canada what your condition means for steady work, not just what it is called.
blocks.extra: The quick check in Section 05 tests whether you can spot the next move.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: What do “severe” and “prolonged” mean for CPP disability?
items.detail: Severe means you regularly cannot do any job that pays a real living. Prolonged means long-term with no end date, or likely to result in death.

items.title: What are the two main CPP payment routes?
items.detail: Usually, payments in four of the past six years, or at least 25 years of payments including three of the past six.

items.title: Why does a DTC approval not mean CPP disability approval?
items.detail: The programs use different legal tests. CPP disability also needs enough CPP payments, and it looks at whether you can regularly work at a job that pays a real living.

items.title: Which three kinds of proof should connect?
items.detail: Medical proof, proof of your daily limits and proof from your work.

items.title: Why send your part of the application without waiting for the medical report?
items.detail: Service Canada needs both parts to decide, but the date it gets your application can affect how far back payments go.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): CPP Disability Evidence and Application Map

blocks.text: Use short labels for your evidence, not full medical records or ID numbers. Keep private papers in a safe file outside this form.
In 2026, contact Service Canada once your work earnings before tax reach $7,400. Earnings below that amount should not affect your benefit. Earnings above it may lead to a review of what you can do.

items.title: CPP disability
items.text: A taxable monthly disability payment for people who paid into CPP.

items.title: Severe
items.text: You regularly cannot do any job that pays a real living.

items.title: Prolonged
items.text: Long-term with no end date, or likely to result in death.

items.title: Substantially gainful
items.text: Work that pays at or above the program’s yearly earnings measure.

items.title: Late applicant
items.text: A possible route if your disability began while your CPP payments still met the rule.

items.title: Retroactive payment
items.text: Back pay for an approved past period.

items.title: Reconsideration
items.text: A formal request, within 90 days, to review a CPP decision.

quiz.question: True or False: “Being unable to return to my old occupation automatically meets the CPP disability test.”

questions: How old are you, and have you checked your CPP Statement of Contributions? (Yes / No / Not sure)
About when did steady work become too hard? A month and year is fine.
Which parts of your job can you no longer do reliably? A few examples are enough.
Have you tried going back to work, or worked reduced hours or changed duties? What happened?
Have you sent your part of the application, and has your doctor sent the medical report? (Both sent / Only mine / Neither yet / Not sure)
What is one thing you will do this week for your application?
samples: Lifting, walking the floor for a full shift, and keeping up a safe pace.
I tried four-hour shifts for two weeks. I needed two days to recover after each one.
Only mine. My doctor’s report is due next month.
Write down every missed shift and change at work since January.
